category: EP Purpose and the ECM Duel
tags: ep purpose and the ecm duel
prompt: A company encrypts all of its radio traffic and considers Electronic Protection complete. What is wrong with this?
options: EP needs several measures together, and encryption does not stop jamming
Nothing is wrong; encryption alone answers the enemy's find, jam and read questions
Only the EW company may declare EP complete for the whole unit's emissions
Encryption is not an EP measure, so the company has done nothing toward EP yet
explanation: Slides 14 and 24: encryption protects what you say but does not stop jamming; hard to find, jam and read requires the measures together.

category: EP Purpose and the ECM Duel
tags: ep purpose and the ecm duel
prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the five EP measures in PAM 3-0702-01, paragraph 0110?
options: Encryption
Pulse compression
Spectrum management
Emission control
explanation: Slide 7: the five measures are hardening, encryption, frequency hopping, emission control and spectrum management; pulse compression is a radar technique (slide 21).

category: EP Purpose and the ECM Duel
tags: ep purpose and the ecm duel
prompt: A student concludes that fielding frequency hopping ends the ECM/ECCM duel. Which statement corrects this?
options: Hopping defeats barrage jamming as well as spot jamming, so the duel ends there and no other layer is needed
Only the enemy needs further layers, because friendly radios are already protected
Hopping makes encryption unnecessary, so the radios can stay in plain mode on every net
The enemy answers hopping with barrage jamming, so protection needs further layers
explanation: Slides 6 and 14: after the radios hop the enemy switches to barrage, and the answer is lower power, terrain masking and PACE.

prompt: A patrol must send a contact report while the enemy is using direction finding. Which transmission best applies radio discipline?
options: Repeated radio checks followed by a full report at a fixed time on the same net
A long encrypted report sent from the hilltop with the antenna on the skyline
Clear voice and fully detailed, at high power so that it surely gets through
Pre-planned, in brevity codes, short, at the lowest power that works
explanation: Slide 9: lowest power that works, short transmissions with pre-planned brevity-coded messages, transmit only when needed.

prompt: Which enemy question is correctly paired with its Electronic Protection answer?
options: Can I FIND you? - Encryption, brevity codes and saying less
Can I FIND you? - Frequency hopping, directional antennas and PACE alternate means
Can I READ you? - Emission control, low power and terrain masking
Can I JAM you? - Frequency hopping, directional antennas and PACE alternate means
explanation: Slide 8: FIND - EMCON, low power, terrain masking; JAM - hopping, directional antennas, PACE; READ - encryption, brevity codes, say less.

prompt: Two company positions must link by radio, with the enemy beyond a ridge to the east. Which arrangement best applies the lesson?
options: A directional antenna aimed at the friendly station, off the skyline, ridge between it and the enemy
A directional antenna aimed east across the ridge toward the enemy side to test for jamming
An omnidirectional antenna raised on the ridge top for the widest coverage of both company positions
A directional antenna on the skyline with camouflage nets over its front and at full power
explanation: Slides 9 and 10: point the energy at your station, keep antennas off skylines and put terrain between the antenna and the enemy.

prompt: A drone control station was located by direction finding and then engaged by indirect fire. Which Ukraine lesson fits?
options: Static emissions get hit
DF leads to fires
Blending works
Move, mask, minimise
explanation: Slide 23: drone control stations were located by direction finding and engaged by indirect fire - DF leads to fires.

prompt: A command post has a hilltop site with wide coverage and a reverse-slope site with weaker coverage, while enemy DF and jammers are active. Which decision follows the lesson?
options: Use the reverse slope; terrain between the antenna and the enemy blocks DF and jamming
Use the hilltop; its wide coverage outweighs the risk of enemy direction finding and jamming
Use the reverse slope and raise power so that the weaker coverage is made up by full power
Use the hilltop and switch to EMCON 1, GREEN once the antenna is raised
explanation: Slides 9 and 10: avoid hilltops for CPs - easy to DF, easy to jam; use the reverse slope or the side of a building.

prompt: The home-on-jam slide gives which lesson for our own emitters?
options: Any strong emitter, jammer or radio, can be located and struck
A jammer is safe from such weapons once its power has been lowered
Weapons guide only on unencrypted emitters, so encrypted radios are safe
Only enemy jammers, and not friendly radios, can be struck by such weapons
explanation: Slide 22: some weapons can switch to guiding on a jamming source, so any strong emitter can be located and struck.

prompt: Attacks are under way and one system shows signs of compromise. Which EMCON level and action follow?
options: EMCON 2, YELLOW, limiting transmissions
EMCON 5, BLACK, isolating the compromised system
EMCON 4, RED, switching non-essential emitters off
EMCON 3, AMBER, turning unencrypted systems off
explanation: Slide 12: EMCON 5, BLACK - attacks are under way, the most restrictive level, with compromised systems isolated.

prompt: Which EMCON level is correctly matched with its condition?
options: EMCON 3, AMBER: a risk has been identified
EMCON 1, GREEN: attacks are under way
EMCON 4, RED: a risk of attack
EMCON 2, YELLOW: an attack has already occurred
explanation: Slide 12: GREEN no hostile activity; YELLOW risk of attack; AMBER risk identified; RED attack has occurred; BLACK attacks under way.

prompt: What does the EMCON slide say about moving between levels?
options: Practice it only during major exercises
Plan it on paper and brief it once to all the units
Rehearse it in every exercise, not just on paper
Leave it to the EW cell
explanation: Slide 12: rehearse moving between levels in every exercise, not just on paper.

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes encryption from anti-jam measures?
options: Encryption and anti-jam measures both protect only what is said
Encryption keeps the link working; anti-jam measures protect what is said
Encryption protects what is said; anti-jam measures keep the link working
Encryption hides the location; anti-jam measures hide the content
explanation: Slide 14: encryption protects WHAT you say; anti-jam protects WHETHER it gets through.

prompt: Radios set to secure mode on a fixed channel are jammed. Which statement best explains the failure and the fix?
options: Secure mode protects delivery of the message, so switch the radios to plain mode on the same fixed channel
Hop mode protects content; keep the fixed channel and raise power
Secure mode causes the jamming; switch off encryption
Secure mode protects content, not delivery; set the radios to HOP as well as SECURE
explanation: Slide 14: your tactical radio gives you both encryption and anti-jam if you set it to HOP and SECURE.

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes frequency hopping from spread spectrum?
options: Hopping protects content; spread spectrum protects the link
Hopping spreads the signal so that it is harder to detect and jam; spread spectrum jumps channels in a pattern only friendly radios know
Hopping jumps channels in a pattern only friendly radios know; spread spectrum spreads the signal so it is harder to detect and jam
Hopping is a radar technique; spread spectrum is a radio technique
explanation: Slide 13: hopping jumps channels many times per second; spread spectrum spreads the signal so it is harder to detect and jam.

prompt: A signaller disconnects the antenna and the noise drops; after moving a short distance the noise changes greatly. Which conclusion fits both results?
options: The source is an equipment fault in the antenna connector
The source is outside the radio, and terrain plays no part
The source is outside the radio, and terrain or direction is involved
The source is the radio's own cables or power, and terrain plays no part in it
explanation: Slide 15: noise that drops means an outside source; a big change after moving means terrain or direction is involved.

prompt: How is an interference report sent when the net is jammed?
options: Directly on the jammed net, using brevity codes so the enemy cannot read it
Through the EW cell alone, not through the S6
To the S3 only, at the next scheduled report time
Through the chain to the S6 and the EW cell, by an alternate means
explanation: Slide 17: send it through the chain to the S6 and the EW cell; use an alternate means if the net is jammed and never in the clear on the jammed net.

prompt: Which interference-report line is correctly paired with its content?
options: EFFECT: the type of signal, such as noise, tones, voice or false signals
FREQUENCY / NET: the affected frequency, net or system such as GPS
ACTIONS: the grid and bearing to the source
WHAT: the date-time group the interference started
explanation: Slide 17: WHEN is the date-time group; WHERE is the grid and bearing; WHAT is the type; EFFECT is what the mission lost; ACTIONS is what you did.

prompt: Which draft reproduces the example PACE plan in the lesson?
options: P: tactical radio, hop and secure; A: HF radio or another net; C: field wire or messenger vehicle; E: runner or visual signals
P: field wire; A: tactical radio; C: HF radio; E: visual signals
P: HF radio or another net; A: tactical radio in hop and secure mode; C: runner or visual signals; E: field wire or messenger vehicle
P: tactical radio in hop and secure mode; A: runner; C: HF radio; E: messenger vehicle
explanation: Slide 18: the example plan runs tactical radio, then HF or another net, then field wire or messenger vehicle, then runner or visual and pyrotechnic signals.

prompt: A patrol's GPS shows a plausible position, but the time is wrong and a speed is shown while the patrol is stationary. Which interpretation and action fit the lesson?
options: Suspect hardening failure; ground the receiver
Accept the position because it looks plausible and continue
Suspect spoofing; cross-check with map, compass and terrain, and report it
Suspect jamming; raise power and keep relying on the GPS position for the whole patrol
explanation: Slide 19: spoofing red flags are position jumps, wrong time and speed while stationary; cross-check with map, compass and terrain and report it.

prompt: Jamming arrives from the side while a radar's main antenna looks ahead. Which technique lets the radar ignore it?
options: Frequency agility, changing frequency pulse to pulse
Sidelobe blanking, with a second antenna spotting the jamming
Low-probability-of-intercept, using low-power waveforms
Pulse compression, squeezing a long coded pulse on receive to reject the jamming
explanation: Slide 21: sidelobe blanking uses a second antenna to spot jamming from the side, and the radar ignores it.

prompt: Which sensor ECCM technique is correctly paired with its effect?
options: Sidelobe blanking: the radar changes frequency from pulse to pulse
Low-probability-of-intercept: low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect
Pulse compression: low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect when transmitted
Frequency agility: a second antenna spots jamming from the side
explanation: Slide 21: LPI uses low-power, wideband waveforms that are hard for ES to detect.
